steps.explanationAfterStep: Initiation: the weak O–O bond breaks homolytically on heating. Only a trace of peroxide is needed, because each radical starts a long chain.
The strong O–H bond formed pays for breaking the weak H–Br bond. Br• is the chain carrier.
Br• adds to the less substituted end, giving the more stable secondary radical. Bromine ends up on the terminal carbon: anti-Markovnikov orientation, set by radical stability, not cation stability.
The radical takes H from HBr and gives back Br•, which adds to the next propene. The two propagation steps repeat until the reagents run out or two radicals meet.

title: Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr
subtitle: With a peroxide, HBr adds to propene by a radical chain and gives 1-bromopropane
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 37 (Radical reactions)

reactants.caption: propene + HBr + a trace of di-tert-butyl peroxide
hintTiers: Which bond in the flask is weakest? Peroxides are used as initiators for a reason.
The O–O bond (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹) breaks on heating, one electron to each oxygen. Two fish-hooks.
One O–O electron → the left oxygen; the other O–O electron → the right oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Initiation. Break the weakest bond with fish-hook arrows.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Without peroxide, HBr adds by the polar route: protonation gives the secondary cation and 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov). With peroxide, a faster radical chain takes over. Start it by breaking the weak O–O bond.
H–Br (about 365 kJ mol⁻¹) is far stronger than the O–O bond of a peroxide. The peroxide is the initiator.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right so far: one electron goes to each oxygen. Draw the second fish-hook.

carbon-radical.caption: secondary 1-bromoprop-2-yl radical + HBr
hintTiers: The carbon radical needs to finish its bonding. HBr has a weak bond to a hydrogen.
The carbon radical takes the hydrogen of HBr; the H–Br bond splits evenly. Three fish-hooks.
Carbon's unpaired electron → new C–H bond; one H–Br electron → C–H; the other → bromine.
carbon-radical.learnerPrompt: Propagation, step 2: the carbon radical meets HBr.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking bromine would leave a hydrogen atom, H•, a very high-energy radical. The carbon radical takes the hydrogen and releases Br•.
Losing Br• again reverses the addition. It does happen, but with HBr present the radical is trapped by hydrogen transfer.
The other tert-butoxyl radical will do exactly that and start a second chain, but follow the radical you have just made.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One more fish-hook: the new C–H bond needs an electron from the H–Br bond as well.

bromine-radical.caption: bromine radical + propene (+ tert-butanol, the other tert-butoxyl radical, HBr)
hintTiers: Radicals add to alkenes. Which end of propene should bromine bond to, to leave the more stable radical?
Bromine bonds to the CH₂ end; one π electron joins it, the other ends on the middle carbon, giving a secondary radical. Three fish-hooks.
Bromine's unpaired electron → new Br–C bond to the CH₂ carbon; one π electron → the same bond; the other π electron → the middle carbon.
bromine-radical.learnerPrompt: Propagation, step 1: the bromine radical adds to the C=C.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Adding to the middle carbon leaves a primary radical on the CH₂ end. Adding to the CH₂ end leaves a more stable secondary radical, and the CH₂ end is also less hindered.
The other tert-butoxyl radical will do exactly that and start a second chain, but follow the radical you have just made.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One more fish-hook: the new C–Br bond needs one electron from the π bond as well.

alkoxyl-radicals.caption: two tert-butoxyl radicals + propene + HBr
hintTiers: An O–H bond is stronger than an H–Br bond. What does the oxygen radical take from HBr?
The oxygen radical takes the hydrogen of HBr; the H–Br bond splits evenly. Three fish-hooks.
Oxygen's unpaired electron → new O–H bond; one H–Br electron → O–H; the other → bromine.
alkoxyl-radicals.learnerPrompt: The alkoxyl radical makes a bromine radical from HBr.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Alkoxyl radicals can add to alkenes, but taking H from the weak H–Br bond is much faster. That gives Br•, which carries the chain.
Taking the bromine would leave H•, a very unstable radical, and make a weak O–Br bond. The oxygen takes the hydrogen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: One more fish-hook: the new O–H bond needs an electron from the H–Br bond too.

mechanismSummary: A peroxide O–O bond breaks on heating. The alkoxyl radical takes H from HBr, making Br•. Br• adds to the CH₂ end of propene to give the more stable secondary radical, which takes H from HBr and releases Br• again. Bromine ends on the terminal carbon: the opposite (anti-Markovnikov) orientation to the polar addition, which goes through the more stable cation. Only HBr does this: for HCl and HI one of the propagation steps is too unfavourable.
